newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada suspends lumber export permits for two days.
newsitem.headline: Canada suspends lumber export permits for two days.

text.p: Canada said on Thursday it suspended the issue of export permits for shipments of softwood lumber to the United States for two days, but that it would resume issuing permits on November 1.

"As you may be aware, the Export/Import Control Bureau did not issue export permits on Wednesday, October 30, 1996, and will not be issuing permits today, October 31, 1996," Claudio Valle, director of the Trade Controls Policy Division at the international trade department, said in a statement.
Valle said the suspension was due to "system modifications respecting quota allocations" which were being completed over the two days.

On Thursday, Canadian lumber companies were to receive their quarterly allocations for softwood lumber shipments to the United States. But government spokeswoman said the quota information would be confidential and it would be up to the companies to release their allocations.
"Permit issuance will resume of Friday, November 1, 1996," Valle said. "Accordingly, daily statistical reports will resume on Monday, November 4, 1996."

Under an agreement between Canada and the United States that took effect on April 1, Canadian lumber shipments that exceed 14.7 billion board feet annually, or 4.226 billion board feet quarterly, are subject to export fees.

During the first two quarters of the agreement, export permits were processed on a first-come, first-served basis, but starting with the third quarter, which began on October 1, export permits are issued according to individual export quotas for very lumber exporting company.

Under the new allocation, lumber exporters based in British Columbia will get 59 percent of the total annual quota, Quebec companies will get 23 percent, Ontario companies 10.3 percent and Alberta exporters 7.7 percent.
The new allocation goes to primary producers and remanufacturers who process lumber further, while wholesalers of lumber are not given direct quotas.
The allocation will be reviewed annually for the next four years of the life of the Canada-U.S. agreement.
-- Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613-235-6745
